placeholders.days: whole days since the relevant event — the student's last visit, a past failure on this problem, or the length of the current unbroken practice streak
placeholders.streak: number of consecutive correct drills in the current run
placeholders.attempts: how many attempts the student previously needed on this problem
placeholders.secret: the name of the secret currently being taught or tested
placeholders.idiom: the C++ expression at the heart of the current secret
placeholders.requirement: name of the gate dimension that is short: recognition, understanding, implementation, or retention
placeholders.shortfall: how far the short gate dimension sits below its threshold, as a percentage
placeholders.score: how many final-test problems were answered correctly
placeholders.total: number of problems in the final test
placeholders.required: how many must be answered correctly to pass

greeting_first: Stand there. I keep a record of everyone who comes through that door and of what they cost me. You are now in it.
You have written programs that read their input once and forgot it. Nothing here forgets. That is the difference, and it is the whole of my region.
I will not ask whether your code works. I will ask what one query costs, and what one update costs, and how many of each the statement intends. Have both numbers ready.
Other masters teach you to find an answer. I teach you to keep one, correct, through two hundred thousand changes. Sit.
greeting_returning: Back. The ledger says where we stopped. Continue from there.
Sit. Cost of a query, cost of an update. Begin.
Again. Nothing has been forgiven since yesterday and nothing has been lost.
You return. Good. Recite the four rows of the table before we start.
greeting_after_gap: {days} days. The record kept itself while you were away; that is what a record is for. You did not.
Gone {days} days. What decays first is not the loops — it is which structure the statement was asking for. We begin there.
{days} days. Answer me now: the smallest value in a range, with the values changing. Which structure, and why not the other one?
{days} days away. I do not ask where you were. I ask what `i & -i` gives you and why the array is one-indexed.
lesson_intro: {secret}. Watch what it costs, not what it does. Everyone remembers what it does.
One structure. Two operations. Learn the price of each before you learn the syntax of either.
This is small. Every structure in this vault is small. The expensive part is choosing the wrong one and finding out at minute fifty.
I name it now, and I will hold you to the cost of it for the rest of your time here.
lesson_memorise: Keep `{idiom}`. Not the idea of it — the characters of it, in order, from memory.
This one you will write under a clock or not at all. There is no time to derive it and there never has been.
Commit it. A structure you can explain and cannot type is a structure you do not have.
Into the hand. The reason goes into the ledger, where I can ask for it later.
drill_wrong: No. That erases every copy. The container did exactly what you asked and you asked for the wrong thing.
Wrong. The default shows the largest. To keep the k largest you hold the smallest of them at the top.
No. Zero is not neutral for a maximum. Your query over negative data answers a number that is not in the array.
Wrong. The lowest set bit of zero is zero, so that loop does not advance. It does not answer badly — it does not stop.
No. A minimum cannot be undone, so there is no pair of prefixes to subtract. You have written an expression that does not exist.
Wrong. You totalled up to the rank itself, so every equal value became a pair out of order. Right on distinct data, and only on distinct data.
drill_streak: {streak} in a row. Speed is cheap. I am still counting the cost per query.
{streak} straight. Do not let fluency become the reason you stop asking what it costs.
trial_intro: Nothing is named. The constraints already told you which structure; read them before the story.
One statement. Decide what one query costs and what one update costs, and the choice makes itself.
The label is off. The bounds are not.
Read it twice. The second reading is for the sentence that says the data changes.
fail_wrong_pattern: Wrong structure. Nothing in that statement was ever written to. A row that never changes wants a table built once, not a promise you never collect on.
No. That question asked HOW MANY lie below the value, not WHICH one. A balanced tree hands you an element and refuses to count.
That quantity has no inverse. You reached for four lines where the answer had to be assembled out of stored pieces, and no subtraction will save it.
No. There were no positions in that statement at all — nothing said where a value sat. You cannot query a range of a bag.
Wrong. The bound of 10^18 was on the interval, not on the input. You built a structure over something nobody asked you to store.
fail_timeout: Time. You knew the structure in the first minute and spent thirty more deciding you were allowed to use it.
Time ran out. That is a fluency debt, and drills are how it is paid. Nothing is lost from the record.
Time. You wrote sixty lines where four would have done, and the four were the ones you knew by heart.
Time. You were deriving the walk. That walk is memorised, or it is not available.
fail_wrong_answer: Right structure. Wrong copy count — erase by value took all three, and no sample with distinct data would ever have shown you.
The walk was correct and the index was zero-based. It did not answer wrongly; it stopped answering.
Correct approach, wrong identity. Zero for a maximum, on data that never went positive.
You had it. prefix(rank) where prefix(rank - 1) was meant — every equal pair counted, and only the test with repeats disagreed.
The tiling was right and the accumulator was an int. Two times ten to the tenth does not fit and the count came back negative.
The structure held. The left endpoint did not: F(r) - F(l) drops it, and only on the inputs where l itself qualifies.
success: Accepted. The next statement gives less away.
Done. The cost was right as well as the answer.
success_fast: Fast, and you named the cost before you named the structure. That is the correct order.
You read the constraints first. That is why it was fast.
No wasted structure and no wasted minutes. Continue.
You refused the heavier tree without arguing with yourself about it. Good.
praise_exceptional: That was well done. You proved the quantity had no inverse before you wrote a line, and everything after that was bookkeeping.
You chose four lines over sixty and could say why. Most students here can only do the second part afterwards.
Clean. You compressed because the mismatch told you to, not because you had seen it done.
The best you have done in this vault. You costed both operations and then wrote the smaller thing.
praise_major: I have watched students build a general tree for a running total and call it thoroughness. You did not. You have earned my respect.
You can now tell in ten seconds which of these structures a statement is describing, and defend the answer. That is rarer than any of the code. You have earned my respect.
I say this once and it goes in the record: you understand what each of these costs, every single query. You have earned my respect.
memorisation_detected: You remember which structure this problem wanted. You cannot say what it would cost on a different one. Those are not the same knowledge. Another problem.
You pass the statements you have seen and fail their variants. That is recall, not judgement. Back one step.
Change the quantity from a sum to a minimum and you are lost, which tells me you learned a shape and not a boundary. Try this.
improvement_noticed: You failed this {days} days ago and solved it today, with the cheaper structure. The record shows both. Continue.
{attempts} attempts on this once. One today. Noted.
This is the problem where you built the general tree for a running total. You did not build it today.
Straighter than last time. You asked whether it could be undone before you asked how to store it.
commitment_noticed: {days} days unbroken. A structure that is correct on the ten-thousandth query is built by someone who returns on the ten-thousandth day.
Many arrive at this vault. Most want the code and not the cost, and most leave when I ask for the cost. You have not.
You have come back after every failure recorded against you. I keep the record precisely so that this can be seen. Keep going.
Quickness arrives here often and forgets the price list by the following week. Attendance I cannot teach, and you brought your own.
gate_locked: Not yet. {requirement} is short by {shortfall} percent. The record does not round in your favour.
The gate holds. Understanding is short — you can build these and not yet say which one a statement is asking for.
No. Recognition is short. Five structures, and you are still deciding by which one you drilled last.
Implementation is short. The choice is right and the walk is written from reasoning rather than from memory. Drill it.
Retention is short. What you held last week has fallen out, and a structure you cannot rebuild in a contest is a structure you never had.
gate_open: The gate is open. Come when the walks are automatic, not when you are impatient.
Nothing is short. The final test is waiting and it names nothing.
You meet every requirement in the record. The decision from here is yours.
final_test_intro: I name nothing. Every drill before this existed so that I would not have to.
{total} statements, {required} of them right. For each one, decide what a query costs and what an update costs. Then write the smaller thing.
No help. Only the constraints, and whatever price list you still carry.
One of these needs no structure at all. Recognising that is also an answer.
victory: {score} of {total}. It is done, and it is written down.
You passed. What you take from this vault is not five structures — it is the habit of costing both operations before you type. Go.
Finished. Everything after this assumes you can tell a subtraction from a merge. You can.
That is mastery of the standing record. Nothing you meet later will be cheaper than what you now know how to refuse. Go.
